strengths: The core insight is clean, well-motivated, and clearly articulated: MDE predictions may be locally accurate but globally misaligned, so a global scale-and-shift is insufficient, and a learned polynomial transformation with inflection points generalizes the affine correction. Figure 1 and the geometric intuition (Sec. 3.1, 3.3) make the idea easy to follow.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art performance on three established benchmarks (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) at three depth ranges, with large margins on ZJU (46.8% MAE) and VoD (31.8% MAE).

A fair-ish backbone-controlled comparison is provided (Tab. 2): even when RadarCam-Depth is given the same UniDepth backbone, PolyRad improves by ~20.8% MAE, indicating the gains come from the polynomial fitting rather than only the foundation model.

Thorough ablations (Tab. 3, 4) covering polynomial degree sensitivity, learnable prototypes vs. self-attention, cross-modality fusion, and the monotonicity regularizer, each showing a measurable contribution.

The first-derivative regularization (Eqs. 8-9) is a sensible and novel training objective connecting polynomial fitting to isotonic regression, addressing the known oscillation problem of high-degree polynomials.
The method is lightweight (predicting N+1 coefficients) and adds negligible inference overhead relative to linear scale-and-shift.
weaknesses: The transformation is a single global 1D polynomial per scene (coefficients are predicted from a GAP-pooled scene vector, Eqs. 5-6), so corrections are purely depth-dependent and cannot correct spatially distinct errors at similar depths. Several claims about 'localized adjustments' and 'correcting fine object boundaries' (Sec. 3.3) overstate what a global polynomial can do; the paper should be more precise about this limitation.

The reported improvement percentages are inconsistent across the paper: the abstract claims 30.3% MAE / 37.2% RMSE, the contributions claim 11.3% / 54.6% / 35.2% across datasets, and Sec. 4.1 claims 12.1% / 46.8% / 31.8% MAE (and RMSE numbers that do not match either). These discrepancies undermine confidence in the reported claims and should be reconciled.

The huge disparity in improvement magnitude between ZJU (46-62%) and nuScenes (~10-12%) is not analyzed. It is unclear whether this reflects dataset characteristics, baseline under-training, or evaluation differences, and this weakens the generality of the SOTA narrative.

Comparison fairness is only partially addressed: in Tab. 1, baselines such as GET-UP, RadarNet, and Lin do not leverage large-scale pretrained MDE backbones, while PolyRad does. The Tab. 2 study mitigates this for RadarCam-Depth only, on nuScenes; equivalent backbone-controlled comparisons on ZJU and VoD are missing.

The argument that polynomial degrees of freedom are 'close to the cardinality of radar point clouds' making the system 'better posed' (Sec. 1, 3.3) is hand-wavy; the number of constraints is the number of ground-truth pixels, not radar points, so the under/over-determination framing is not rigorously justified.

The monotonicity regularizer only softly encourages d(d̂)/dz ≈ 1 on average; it does not guarantee monotonicity, yet the paper repeatedly claims it 'enforces' or 'ensures' monotonicity. The interplay of λ1-λ3 weights and the sensitivity to these weights are not reported in the main text.

Reproducibility is limited from the main paper: no code release is mentioned, key hyperparameters (λ weights, number of prototypes, training details) are deferred to a supplementary not visible here, and the choice of UniDepth as the default backbone raises dependence concerns if that model changes.

Some claims of broader significance ('no prior work has explored polynomial fitting for adapting predictions of pretrained foundation models... a novel solution for any task that leverages foundation models') are speculative and unsupported by experiments beyond depth estimation.

strengths: The core idea is simple, efficient, and well-motivated: instead of per-pixel depth completion (underdetermined given sparse radar) or a global affine fit (overconstrained), a global polynomial in the scaleless MDE prediction offers a tunable middle ground with few degrees of freedom. This is an appealing formulation.

Empirical evidence is reasonably broad: consistent SOTA across three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) at three evaluation ranges (Table 1), across four MDE backbones (Table 2), with component ablations (Table 4) and a degree sensitivity study (Table 3).

The first-derivative regularization encouraging d(d̂)/dz ≈ 1 is a sensible inductive bias that connects to isotonic regression and addresses the well-known oscillation problem of high-degree polynomial fits; the ablation confirms it matters.
The paper is mostly well-written, and the geometric discussion of inflection points and coefficient signs provides intuition for an otherwise opaque regression head.
weaknesses: Internal numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence: the abstract claims improvements of 30.3% MAE and 37.2% RMSE, while the contributions list 11.3%, 54.6%, and 35.2% per dataset, and Section 4.1 reports 12.1%/10.5% on nuScenes. These figures cannot all be correct, which is a credibility problem for a paper whose main claim is empirical superiority.

Potential unfairness in the headline comparison: Table 1 reports RadarCam-Depth at 1689.7 MAE, which matches 'RadarCam-Depth w/ DPT' in Table 2, while PolyRad's headline result uses the stronger UniDepth backbone (1454.1). The like-for-like comparison (both with UniDepth, 1872.0 vs 1454.1, Table 2) shows a real but considerably smaller gain (~22%) than the abstract suggests. This should be stated transparently.

The method's expressiveness is narrower than the motivation implies. The transform is a single polynomial applied purely as a function of the scaleless depth value z, with one global coefficient vector per scene (after GAP). It therefore cannot correct cross-object misalignment when MDE assigns similar z to objects at different true depths, nor perform any spatially varying correction. The Fig. 1 narrative ('three or more objects') overstates what the model can do; the actual capability is limited to correcting errors that are a monotone function of z.

There is an unanalyzed tension between the motivation and the regularization: the L1 penalty on (1 − d̂d/dz) is applied across the whole scene, yet the method's premise is that corrections must be large and non-uniform in certain depth ranges. Pulling the derivative toward 1 everywhere works against exactly the depth-dependent stretching the paper advocates, and no analysis quantifies how this trade-off behaves.

Some claims are overreaching or weakly supported: 'no prior work has explored polynomial fitting for adapting predictions of pretrained foundation models' ignores related non-linear alignment ideas; the argument that polynomial degrees of freedom are 'close to the cardinality of radar point clouds' is hand-wavy and does not follow from any stated principle.

Evaluation breadth is limited: only MAE and RMSE are reported (no δ-threshold metrics common in depth estimation), baseline numbers appear to be taken from prior papers rather than re-run under identical conditions, and key implementation details (training schedule, λ weights, degree selection protocol) are deferred to supplementary material not present in the manuscript, weakening reproducibility.

The learned degree-1 configuration (Table 3: 2156.8 MAE) performs worse than the raw median-scaled UniDepth prediction (2129.8), which suggests the fusion architecture itself, rather than polynomial fitting alone, contributes substantially to the gains; the paper does not disentangle these effects beyond the degree sweep.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: replacing a global scale-and-shift correction of MDE predictions with a learned polynomial transformation, motivated by the observation that MDE models get local structure right but misalign regions relative to each other (Fig. 1, Sec. 3.1).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on three standard radar-camera benchmarks (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) at multiple maximum-depth settings, with consistent improvements over five recent baselines (Table 1).

Useful comparative studies: the method is tested with four different MDE backbones (Table 2), showing the polynomial fitting mechanism (not a particular backbone) drives the gains, and the polynomial-degree sensitivity study (Table 3) shows a sensible capacity/overfitting trade-off with a plausible degradation at degree 10.

Ablation studies (Table 4) isolate the contribution of each architectural component and the monotonicity loss, and the qualitative results (Figs. 3-4) are informative, including error maps and visualizations of the learned polynomial curves.
The first-derivative regularization to suppress oscillatory high-degree polynomials is a reasonable and interpretable inductive bias, connected to isotonic regression.
The method is lightweight (an MLP predicting N+1 coefficients) compared to complex multi-stage radar-camera fusion systems, and the frozen MDE backbone avoids large-scale data collection.
weaknesses: The central conceptual claim is not fully supported by the method as formulated. Because the coefficients are predicted from a globally pooled scene representation (Eq. 5-6), the transformation is a single scalar function of the scaleless depth z. It can therefore only correct cross-object misalignment when objects differ in their scaleless depth values; two regions assigned similar z by the MDE model cannot be separated regardless of radar evidence. The paper's framing (Fig. 1) implies richer spatially varying corrections than the architecture can actually express. A learned monotone calibration baseline (e.g., a small monotone MLP, piecewise-linear/spline fit, or per-depth-band linear corrections guided by radar) is the obvious comparator for the polynomial form and is missing; without it, the benefit of specifically a polynomial parameterization is not established.

The monotonicity regularizer (Eq. 8, third term) penalizes ||1 - dd̂/dz||_1 over the whole scene, i.e., it pulls the derivative toward 1 everywhere. This pushes the transformation toward a global scale-and-shift, arguably working against the very non-uniform corrections the method claims to enable, and the claim that it 'allows' cross-object corrections while preserving local ordering is asserted rather than demonstrated. Also, a soft penalty toward derivative ≈ 1 does not enforce monotonicity (the sign of the derivative is unconstrained), so the stated connection to isotonic regression is overstated. The ablation shows the term helps empirically, but the mechanistic explanation needs tightening.

The degree-of-freedom argument (Sec. 3.3) is hand-wavy: the claim that N+1 polynomial coefficients are 'close to the cardinality of radar point clouds' motivates the approach, yet N is a fixed hyperparameter (chosen as 8) and is not tied to NC in any experiment, so the well-posedness argument is rhetorical rather than demonstrated.

Inconsistencies in the reported improvement claims undermine confidence: the abstract states 30.3% MAE / 37.2% RMSE improvement, while the contributions list 11.3%, 54.6%, and 35.2% across datasets. Both cannot describe the same comparison; the reader cannot tell which baselines and settings these percentages refer to. Additionally, RadarCam-Depth's nuScenes MAE differs between Table 1 (1286.1) and Table 2 (1689.7/1872.0) without clear explanation of which backbone/protocol applies in each table, raising fairness questions about the headline comparison.

The magnitude of the ZJU improvement (46.8% MAE over the previous best) is strikingly larger than on the other two datasets; no analysis is offered for why one benchmark benefits so disproportionately, and the paper would be stronger with error analysis by depth range or scene content (e.g., does the gain come mostly from far-range ground regions?).

The novelty framing overreaches: 'no prior work has explored polynomial fitting for adapting predictions of pretrained foundation models' and 'first to formulate radar-camera depth estimation as a scene-fitting problem.' Polynomial/affine alignment and learned calibration of depth predictions are established tools; the honest contribution is applying a polynomial parameterization with a derivative regularizer in this pipeline, which is still valuable but should be claimed more modestly.

The related-work contrast that existing methods 'rely on complex architectures' while PolyRad is 'streamlined' is somewhat rhetorical; PolyRad still includes radar aggregation with learnable prototypes, cross-modality attention, a depth encoder, CNN, and MLPs, and no efficiency/runtime comparison is provided to substantiate the efficiency claim.

Reproducibility details are deferred to supplementary material (datasets, training protocol, code availability is not mentioned in the main text); the main paper alone lacks sufficient implementation detail (e.g., λ1, λ2, λ3 values, NP, feature dimensions, training schedule).

strengths: Novel and clearly articulated formulation: recasting radar-camera metric depth estimation as a scene-fitting problem where a low-dimensional (N+1 parameter) polynomial transforms scaleless MDE predictions, with a well-argued rationale that the degrees of freedom should match the cardinality of sparse radar point clouds rather than the pixel count.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) at multiple distance thresholds, with SOTA results, plus extensive ablations: polynomial degree sensitivity (Tab. 5), architecture/loss ablations (Tab. 6), MDE backbone studies (Tabs. 4, 9, 10), zero-shot cross-dataset generalization (Tab. 11), robustness to reduced radar density (Tab. 12), and comparisons against depth completion methods, regression baselines (isotonic, PCHIP, splines), and adapter fine-tuning (Tab. 13).
Strong efficiency results: lowest inference time (24.81 ms, ~40 fps) and GFLOPs (89.70) among all compared methods, making the contribution practically relevant for real-time deployment.

The first-derivative (monotonicity) regularizer is a sensible and evaluated design choice for stabilizing high-degree polynomial fitting, supported by Kendall's tau analysis with a bootstrap significance test (Tab. G discussion, tau = 0.969 vs. baselines).
Well-written and clearly structured; qualitative figures (Figs. 3, 4, 6) with error maps effectively illustrate where affine correction fails and how the learned transformation behaves.
weaknesses: The transformation is a per-scene, depth-only (1D) function: since coefficients are predicted from a globally pooled representation and applied via Eq. 5, all pixels with the same MDE depth z receive the same metric depth regardless of location or object identity. This limits the claimed ability to correct 'cross-region misalignments between objects' — objects mistakenly assigned identical or near-identical scaleless depths cannot be separated, and the motivating narrative (Fig. 1, Sec. 3.1) somewhat oversells this capability.

Gains over the strongest baseline (TacoDepth) on nuScenes are modest (e.g., 3.1% MAE at 50m, 4.6% at 80m), while the headline '24.9% MAE / 33.2% RMSE' average is dominated by the larger margins on the smaller ZJU and VoD datasets; no statistical significance testing is provided for the main comparisons.

The 'proof' in Appendix H is trivial — three non-collinear points admit no affine fit — yet is presented as significant theoretical justification, and the Corollary's appeal to Taylor expansion provides no actual capacity guarantee relevant to the experimental setting.

The monotonicity regularizer (Eq. 6) targets d(d̂)/dz near 1 rather than merely positive, which penalizes legitimate large global scale corrections and sits in some tension with the stated goal of allowing strong non-uniform adjustments; the trade-off and choice of lambda_mono = 0.25 are not analyzed.

The polynomial degree N is tuned per dataset as a hyperparameter (degree 8 selected), with no clear protocol on validation splits; this reduces clarity of the comparison against baselines that do not require such tuning, and no code release or reproducibility statement is provided.

The reported comparisons use ground truth derived from projected lidar, and evaluation is limited to MAE/RMSE; standard ordinal metrics (e.g., delta < 1.25) or edge/structure metrics that would directly probe the paper's structural-consistency claims are absent from the main evaluation.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and effective: replacing a global affine (scale-and-shift) correction of MDE predictions with a learned per-scene polynomial transform, guided by cheap radar data. This is a sensible middle ground between a 2-DOF affine fit and an ill-posed per-pixel completion, and the underdetermined/overdetermined framing in Sec. 3.3 is a useful way to reason about capacity.

Empirical support is substantial: consistent state-of-the-art MAE/RMSE across three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) at three evaluation distances, plus strong efficiency results (24.81 ms inference, 89.70 GFLOPs, lowest training time). The breadth of evaluation is above average for this area.

Ablations and sensitivity studies are thorough: polynomial degree sweep (Tab. 5), component ablations (Tab. 6), MDE backbone swaps (Tabs. 4, 9, 10), zero-shot cross-dataset transfer (Tab. 11), robustness to reduced radar density (Tab. 12), and comparison against natural non-learned baselines (isotonic regression, PCHIP, splines) and adapter-based alternatives (Tab. 13).

The Kendall's tau monotonicity analysis with bootstrap significance testing (Sec. G) is a thoughtful way to validate the claim that the first-derivative regularizer corrects depth-order inversions, going beyond raw error metrics.

Comparison to lidar depth completion methods (BPNet, NLSPN) applied to radar data, with a clear explanation of why densification approaches fail on sparse/noisy radar, adds useful context for the design choice.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is oversold. 'Proposition 1' and its 'proof by construction' merely observe that three non-collinear points cannot be fit by a line — this is elementary and does not need formal framing. Corollary 1's appeal to Taylor expansion is hand-wavy: a global polynomial in the scalar z assumes metric depth is a function of scaleless depth alone, which is a strong and unexamined assumption (two pixels with the same z but different true depths receive identical corrections, so spatially-varying errors at matched depth values cannot be fixed).

The monotonicity regularizer (Eq. 6-7) appears technically mis-specified relative to its stated purpose. Penalizing |1 - d d̂/dz| drives the derivative toward 1, i.e., toward d̂ ≈ z + const (a pure shift), not merely toward monotonicity. Enforcing approximate monotonicity would require constraining the derivative's sign, not its proximity to the identity derivative. As written, the regularizer conceptually conflicts with the claimed 'stretching/compressing' behavior that motivates the polynomial.

There are internal inconsistencies that undermine confidence: the abstract claims an average improvement of 24.9% MAE / 33.2% RMSE while the introduction claims 29.1%; and Table 6's 'no ablations' row for VoD (629.6/1171.3) exactly repeats the ZJU numbers rather than the reported VoD results (~1500/3960), suggesting a copy error or unverified table.

Fairness of the main comparison is not fully established. It is unclear whether baseline numbers in Tab. 1 are from the original papers or retrained under identical settings, and whether baselines benefit from the same strong MDE foundation-model priors that POLAR uses. Notably, in Tab. 5 the learned degree-1 (scale+shift) variant (MAE 2156.8) performs worse than raw median-scaled UniDepth (2129.8), which is surprising and warrants explanation, especially given that several cited works use exactly this affine correction successfully.

The claim of being 'the first to explore polynomial fitting for adapting predictions of pretrained foundation models' is overstated; fitting polynomial/spline corrections to align predicted relative depth with sparse metric points has appeared in prior monocular depth and radar-ordinal-regression work (e.g., Lo & Vandewalle, 2021), and this novelty claim should be scoped more carefully.

Because coefficients are predicted from a globally average-pooled scene representation, the entire correction is a single 1D curve per frame; the paper's motivating example (Fig. 1, object-level misalignment) implies corrections depend on which object a pixel belongs to, but the model can only modulate correction through the depth value itself. A more explicit analysis of when this assumption fails (e.g., scenes where distinct objects occupy overlapping depth ranges) would strengthen the paper.

The degree N is a hand-tuned hyperparameter that differs in effect across datasets (Tab. 5), limiting out-of-the-box applicability; the limitation is acknowledged but the sensitivity is material (degree 10 degrades nuScenes by ~4% MAE).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: affine scale-and-shift corrections to MDE predictions are insufficient when three or more scene regions are misaligned, and the paper convincingly argues (Fig. 1, Fig. 3, and the degree-sensitivity study in Tab. 5) that a learned polynomial transformation provides a useful middle ground between a 2-DOF affine fit and an ill-posed per-pixel correction.

Strong empirical support: consistent state-of-the-art results across three datasets (nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, View-of-Delft) at multiple evaluation ranges, with the largest margins on ZJU (38.5% MAE) and VoD (31.8% MAE); the method also beats lidar depth-completion methods (BPNet, NLSPN) repurposed for radar, supporting the claim that radar sparsity/elevation ambiguity requires a different approach.

Comprehensive supporting experiments: ablations of each component (Tab. 6), polynomial-degree sensitivity (Tab. 5), four MDE backbones (Tabs. 4, 9, 10), zero-shot cross-dataset transfer (Tab. 11), robustness to reduced radar density (Tab. 12), comparisons against learnable points, adapter tuning, and isotonic/spline regression baselines (Tab. 13), plus statistical significance testing of the monotonicity claim (Kendall's tau with bootstrap t-test, p=0.012).

Excellent efficiency profile: 24.81 ms inference (40.3 fps), 89.70 GFLOPs, and lowest training time per epoch, making the method genuinely attractive for real-time deployment; the overhead analysis of additional polynomial terms (Sec. B) is thorough.

The first-derivative monotonicity regularizer is a simple but sensible inductive bias, and the paper quantitatively verifies that the learned transform actually increases ordinal consistency with ground truth relative to raw MDE predictions (τ=0.969 vs 0.957).
weaknesses: The theoretical framing is overstated. Proposition 1 merely restates that three non-collinear points do not lie on a line—this is a trivial algebraic observation, not a meaningful result, and Corollary 1's appeal to Taylor expansion is hand-wavy (it says nothing about the coefficient budget, radar supervision, or generalization). The paper would be stronger if it presented this as intuition rather than a 'principled geometric formulation.'

A global polynomial in z predicted from a globally pooled (GAP) scene descriptor is fundamentally a 1D remapping of depth values; it cannot spatially disambiguate two objects assigned the same scaleless depth. The narrative that this 'corrects cross-region misalignments between objects' is only partially supported—a polynomial can only shift entire depth-value bands, and Fig. 3/Fig. 4, while suggestive, do not isolate this mechanism from generic fitting.

The marginal gains on nuScenes (4.4% MAE, 3.7% RMSE over TacoDepth) are small relative to the abstract's headline of '24.9% average MAE' improvement, which is dominated by ZJU/VoD results. The paper does not report variance over multiple runs or significance tests for the main benchmark comparisons, so the SOTA claim on nuScenes rests on single-run numbers near baseline noise.

Possible inconsistency in Table 6: the 'no ablations' row lists 629.6/1171.3 under the VoD columns, but these are the ZJU results; the VoD full-model numbers should be 1500.1/3960.5 per Tab. 10. This should be corrected or explained.

It is unclear whether TacoDepth—the closest competitor on nuScenes—was evaluated with the same strong UniDepth backbone, or whether the Tab. 1 comparison mixes backbone configurations. The backbone study covers RadarCam-Depth and POLAR but not TacoDepth.

The monotonicity regularizer pulls d(d̂)/dz toward 1 globally (Eq. 7), which is a global (not 'piecewise monotonic') constraint; the text's characterization is imprecise, and the trade-off between this regularizer's weight and cross-region correction capacity is not analyzed beyond the λ_mono value in Sec. F.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no mention of code release, and several architectural details (prototype count N_P, dimensions c_r/c_z/c_s, CNN f_s design, per-dataset polynomial degrees) are scattered or unspecified, which would hamper exact reproduction.
